I have been farming this land for 35 years. I am 54 now, and I started when I was 19 right after primary school. I have 64 mu in Quzhou, which is a lot of land to manage. My wife works with me in the fields, but my son and daughter-in-law work in the textile factory in town, so when it gets busy I hire people from the village — especially for cotton picking and wheat harvest. I have a well for irrigation, which is my lifeline because the rain here is never enough, especially in spring.

For my wheat, I planted 18 mu last October. I always buy improved seed from the dealer at the market — the "Jimai" type that most people around here plant. Last fall I already spread one bag of compound fertilizer per mu as base. Now that it is turning green, I will broadcast half a bag of urea per mu — that's 25 kg. The input dealer told me this works out to about 18 kg of nitrogen, 6 kg of phosphorus, and 4 kg of potassium per mu for the whole season. I don't do the math myself, but I have bought from this dealer for ten years and his numbers seem right. I will irrigate three times: once at green-up, once at jointing, and once when the grain is filling. I spray twice for aphids and powdery mildew. I don't till the wheat land in spring — that was done last fall. Last year I got about 450 kg per mu, and this year I expect 480 kg if the dry wind doesn't come.

My corn goes on the same 18 mu right after we cut the wheat in early June. You cannot plant corn without hybrid seed now — the old types are finished. I hire a tractor with a rotary tiller the same day we harvest the wheat, and we plant immediately so we don't lose time. At planting I put down 30 kg of compound fertilizer per mu. When the corn reaches the big trumpet stage, I topdress with 20 kg of urea per mu. The dealer says that's 17 kg nitrogen, 5 kg phosphorus, and 4 kg potassium per mu total. I irrigate twice — once right after planting if it is dry, and once at the tasseling stage. I spray three times because corn borers and armyworms always come in July and August. I expect 550 kg per mu.

Cotton is my main crop and my biggest worry. I have 30 mu of cotton. I plough deep in April before planting — cotton roots need loose soil. I use improved cotton seed, the "guoxin" type that my neighbor Lao Zhang used last year and got good bolls on. For fertilizer, I spread one bag of compound fertilizer per mu as base. Then I topdress twice with urea: 15 kg per mu when the flowers open, and another 15 kg per mu when the bolls are setting. I also add 15 kg of potassium sulfate per mu at flowering because cotton needs potassium for the bolls — I learned that from the dealer three years ago. That comes to about 21 kg nitrogen, 7 kg phosphorus, and 9 kg potassium per mu. Cotton drinks a lot of water, so I irrigate four times, especially during flowering and boll stage. Pesticides are where I spend the most. I spray eight times — bollworm, aphids, and red spider mites never stop. Last year I got 260 kg of seed cotton per mu. This year I want 280 kg, but I am worried about the bollworm.

Stevia is something I started two years ago. A buyer from Shandong came to our village and signed a contract to buy dried leaves, so now I have 16 mu. It is easier than cotton. I spread about one bag of compound fertilizer per mu at planting, and topdress once with 10 kg of urea. The dealer says that is 15 kg nitrogen, 5 kg phosphorus, and 6 kg potassium per mu. I irrigate four times and spray twice for insects. I expect about 300 kg of dried leaves per mu.

I always start from what I did last year. Last year fertilizer prices were high, but I still bought everything I needed because a bad harvest is a disaster. Wasting some fertilizer is just money lost; losing half my cotton yield means I cannot pay for my grandchildren's school. With 64 mu, I buy fertilizer by the half-ton to get a better price. I watch what Lao Zhang and the other neighbors do — if everyone is adding more potassium to cotton this year, I think about it. But mostly I stick with what worked before. Change is risky, and I have a household of six people to feed.
